body: 3. Q2 2026 Asset Allocation outlook: Adapting to uncertainty. ***The following is the introduction to our Q2 2026 Asset Allocation outlook***. Bond and equity markets have started to worry about an inflation shock reminiscent of that seen in 2022 or, for those with longer memories, the twin oil crises of the 1970s. The fuller quote highlights the recency bias which makes it difficult to place things in their appropriate historical context: “We are living in most interesting times … I never remember a time in which our history was so full … of new objects of interest, and new objects for anxiety” (Joseph Chamberlain, 1898). When investing, we need to fight the kneejerk tendency to always worry about ‘new objects for anxiety’ and instead focus on the implications of recent events for the fundamentals. However, the sharp backwardation in major commodity markets (i.e. prices in the near future being significantly higher than prices in the distant future) points to a time-limited interruption to global energy supply. As an asset allocation team, we came into this conflict significantly underweight credit in our dynamic funds.

“Boy, that escalated quickly!” While we don’t want to trivialize the Middle East war or the sell-off in markets since February, this memorable line uttered by Will Ferrell in *Anchorman* is one cheeky way to describe the about-face in market returns and risk appetite relative to January’s optimistic outlook. Despite the headwinds, we maintain our moderately overweight view on global equities over our 12-month horizon, for several reasons: The year began with strong earnings momentum, the AI innovation theme remains intact, valuations are more attractive, and fiscal policy remains supportive. We see some risk that markets are not pricing in the possibility of a more prolonged conflict and its economic spillover effects, but we also recognize that global markets entered the crisis with a healthy earnings buffer (quite different from the weakening in earnings leading into last year’s tariff shock) and that we could just as well see a de-escalation in the conflict.
